method: Independent engineering derivations, numerical recomputation, dimensional checks and primary teaching references. Not certified against official UPSC answer keys.

questions.title: Heat flux through furnace lining
questions.solution: q″ = kΔT/L = 0.03 × 200/0.1 = 60 W/m². Area is not specified, so the result is heat flux, not total heat rate.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Thermal resistance of a wall
questions.solution: R = L/(kA) = 0.6/(0.4 × 1.5) = 1 K/W. The temperature difference affects heat rate, not resistance.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Heat flux through a plane wall
questions.solution: The heat-flux magnitude is k|ΔT|/L = 0.51 × 25/0.2 = 63.75 W/m². Heat flows from the hotter outside surface towards the cooler inside.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins
NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Volumetric heat generation in a wire
questions.solution: Use centimetres consistently: V = π(0.3²/4) × 80 = 5.6549 cm³. q‴ = 1200/V = 212.21 W/cm³, nearest option A.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Heat diffusion equation in a cylinder
questions.solution: For steady radial conduction in a solid cylinder with constant k and uniform volumetric generation g, energy balance gives (1/r) d/dr(r dT/dr) + g/k = 0. The generation term cannot be omitted.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Centre temperature of a heated wire
questions.solution: Uniform generation gives T₀ − Tₛ = q‴r₀²/(4k), with q‴ = P/(πr₀²L). Thus T₀ = 105 + 2000/(4π × 15 × 0.5) = 126.22 °C.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Equivalent contact resistance thickness
questions.solution: Contact resistance per unit area is 1/hc; plate resistance per unit area is L/k. Equating them gives L = k/hc = 237/11000 = 0.021545 m = 2.1545 cm.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Lumped temperature assumption
questions.solution: A perfectly uniform internal temperature requires zero internal conduction resistance. The practical lumped approximation uses small, nonzero Biot number (commonly Bi < 0.1); the exact limiting answer here is 0.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Heat flux through a brick wall

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Two-dimensional steady conduction
questions.solution: In Cartesian coordinates, steady 2D conduction with constant conductivity and no heat generation gives the Laplace equation: ∂²T/∂x² + ∂²T/∂y² = 0.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Surface temperature from heat flux
questions.solution: Fourier law gives q″ = −k dT/dx = −25 × (−9000) = 225000 W/m². At the surface, q″ = h(Tₛ − T∞), so Tₛ = 30 + 225000/345 = 682.174 °C.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Equivalent aluminium thickness
questions.solution: Equate L/k = 1/hc. L = 237/10000 = 0.0237 m = 2.37 cm. The thickness of the existing plates is not needed for this equivalent resistance.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, conduction and fins

questions.title: Symmetry of finite fins
questions.solution: By symmetry, the midpoint of the 2l rod has zero axial temperature gradient. Each half has the same length, material, diameter, base temperature and environment as the shorter insulated-tip rod. Its midpoint temperature is therefore 55 °C.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, critical radius and fins

questions.title: Critical diameter of a spherical sheath
questions.solution: For a sphere, critical outer radius r꜀ = 2k/h = 2 × 0.04/10 = 0.008 m. The critical diameter is 2r꜀ = 16 mm, not the thickness of insulation.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, critical radius and fins

questions.title: Insulation thickness for maximum heat loss
questions.solution: For a cylinder, r꜀ = k/h = 0.174/8 = 0.02175 m = 21.75 mm. Existing wire radius is 8/2 = 4 mm. Insulation thickness = 21.75 − 4 = 17.75 mm.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, critical radius and fins

questions.title: Purpose of fins
questions.solution: A fin provides additional exposed area, increasing convective heat transfer when the fin is effective. Its primary purpose is to enlarge the effective surface area.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, critical radius and fins

questions.title: Critical radius around a circular pipe
questions.solution: For a circular pipe, r꜀ = k/h = 0.17/3 = 0.056667 m = 5.67 cm. This is the critical outer radius, not the added insulation thickness.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, critical radius and fins

questions.title: One-dimensional fin validity
questions.solution: Transverse temperature differences must be small for a one-dimensional fin model. The stated criterion uses hδ/k < 0.2, a dimensionless transverse Biot-type quantity. hk/δ is not dimensionless.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat transfer, critical radius and fins
NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Convective heat loss from a sphere
questions.solution: h = Nu k/D. Sphere area A = πD². Thus Q = Nu k πD ΔT = 31.4 × 0.026 × π × 0.012 × 50 = 1.539 W, nearest option D.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Forced-convection dimensionless groups
questions.solution: For forced convection with buoyancy neglected and geometry fixed, Nu is correlated with Reynolds and Prandtl numbers. Grashof number characterizes buoyancy-driven flow.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Liquid metal boundary layers
questions.solution: Pr = ν/α. Liquid metals have very high thermal diffusivity and therefore low Prandtl number; thermal diffusion extends beyond the momentum boundary layer.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Fluid properties in convection
questions.solution: Dynamic viscosity, conductivity and density are fluid properties entering convection correlations. Rate of convection is the resulting heat-transfer rate, not a fluid property.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Turbulent flat-plate correlations
questions.solution: For a turbulent flat-plate boundary layer, the conventional local correlations scale with Reₓ^(−1/5): δ ≈ 0.382x/Reₓ^(1/5), Cƒ ≈ 0.0592/Reₓ^(1/5). The 0.664/Reₓ^0.5 expression belongs to laminar flow.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Hydrodynamic entrance region
questions.solution: The hydrodynamic entrance region is the portion of the tube where the velocity boundary layer develops until it meets at the centreline. Entry length measures the length of that region; the question asks for the region.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Dittus–Boelter correlation
questions.solution: The Dittus–Boelter form is NuD = 0.023 ReD^0.8 Pr^n. Conventionally n = 0.4 for heating the fluid and 0.3 for cooling, within the correlation’s applicability limits.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Reynolds number of hot water flow
questions.solution: Use the inside diameter and convert velocity: 25 cm/s = 0.25 m/s. Re = ρVD/μ = 960 × 0.25 × 0.0525/(2.82×10⁻⁴) = 44680.85, nearest option B.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Tube-side convection coefficient
questions.solution: h = Nu k/D = 151.4 × 0.68/0.0525 = 1960.99 W/(m²·K). A temperature difference of 1 °C equals a difference of 1 K, so printed options A and B are physically equivalent. Either receives full credit in this practice lab.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.editorial: Printed choices A and B use equivalent temperature-difference units. Either is accepted for full credit.

questions.title: Rayleigh, Grashof and Prandtl numbers
questions.solution: By definition, Rayleigh number is the product of Grashof and Prandtl numbers: Ra = Gr Pr.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Natural-convection dominance
questions.solution: Ri = Gr/Re² compares buoyancy with inertia. Natural convection dominates for Ri > 10; forced convection dominates for Ri < 0.1. The middle range involves mixed convection.

sources.title: Rose-Hulman · Combined forced/natural convection

questions.title: Factors affecting convection coefficient
questions.solution: Convection coefficient depends on fluid properties (including viscosity), flow velocity and surface geometry. All three statements are correct.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.title: Heater temperature at reduced heat flux
questions.solution: Assuming the convection coefficient stays constant, h = 5000/(130 − 50) = 62.5 W/(m²·K). Then Tₛ = 50 + 2500/62.5 = 90 °C.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.editorial: Practice assumption: take the convection coefficient as constant when the power changes.

questions.title: Laminar natural-convection range
questions.solution: The conventional laminar natural-convection correlation for a vertical plate is commonly used over 10⁴ < RaL < 10⁹. Transition near 10⁹ depends on geometry and disturbances; this is not a universal criterion for every flow.

sources.title: NPTEL · Flow classifications

questions.editorial: Interpret the listed range as the conventional vertical-plate natural-convection range; geometry is not specified in the printed question.

questions.title: Non-condensable air in condensers
questions.solution: Air remains non-condensable, accumulates near the condensing interface, adds diffusion/thermal resistance and reduces the condensation coefficient. The four listed statements describe those effects.

sources.title: NPTEL · Non-condensable gases and condensation

options: Statement 3: air accumulates near the surface

questions.title: Film boiling and condensation
questions.solution: Film boiling places a continuous vapour layer between the wall and liquid. Film condensation places a condensate layer between wall and vapour. In this film-mediated sense, film boiling is the reverse analogue of film condensation.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

questions.title: Nusselt condensation assumptions
questions.solution: Nusselt’s classical laminar-film model neglects inertia relative to viscous and gravity forces and treats heat transport through the film as conduction. It assumes negligible vapour shear, not very high vapour velocity. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

options: Statement 2: heat crosses the film mainly by conduction
Statement 3: vapour velocity is very high

questions.title: Why transition-boiling heat flux falls
questions.solution: Beyond critical heat flux, increasing vapour coverage impedes contact between liquid and heater. Vapour has lower conductivity than liquid, so the transition-boiling heat flux falls. Statement 2 explains this; statement 1 gives an inappropriate temperature range and statement 3 does not describe the mechanism.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

questions.title: Promoting high condensation coefficients
questions.solution: Dropwise condensation repeatedly exposes parts of the surface instead of maintaining an insulating liquid film, producing larger heat-transfer coefficients.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

questions.title: Air-cooled condenser temperature
questions.solution: Q = hA(Tref − Troom). Using the consistent kJ/hr units: Tref = 25 + 5235/(50 × 6) = 42.45 °C.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

questions.title: Nucleate boiling statements
questions.solution: Nucleate boiling gives high heat-transfer rates, and heat flux rises strongly with surface superheat. A blanket upper limit of 1 MW/m² for water is false; critical heat flux depends on conditions. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

questions.title: Dropwise versus filmwise condensation
questions.solution: The intended textbook comparison is about 10 times the filmwise condensation rate, so D is the best listed choice. This factor is approximate and depends on the surface and operating conditions, not a universal constant.

sources.title: NPTEL · Condensation and boiling
Srinix · Boiling and condensation teaching notes

questions.editorial: The multiplier is an approximate textbook comparison, not a universal physical constant.

questions.title: Electrical power during boiling
questions.solution: Use the wire’s lateral area A = πDL = π × 0.001 × 0.1 m². P = hAΔT = 5000 × A × (114 − 100) = 21.991 W.

questions.title: Sphere inside a cubical enclosure
questions.solution: The convex sphere sees only the enclosure: F₁₂ = 1. Sphere area A₁ = πd² and inner cube area A₂ = 6d². Reciprocity gives F₂₁ = A₁F₁₂/A₂ = π/6.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: Combined radiation and convection heat loss
questions.solution: Per unit length, Q/L = πD[h(Tₛ − T∞) + εσ(Tₛ⁴ − Tsur⁴)]. Use kelvin for radiation: Tₛ ≈ 523 K, Tsur ≈ 303 K. Substitution gives about 818.8 W/m, option B.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: Wavelength of maximum emission
questions.solution: Wien displacement gives λmax = 2898/T = 2898/900 = 3.22 μm, nearest option B. Surface area does not affect the peak wavelength.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: View factor of a hemispherical furnace
questions.solution: The flat floor cannot see itself, hence F₂₁ = 1. Roof area is 2πr² and floor area is πr². Reciprocity gives F₁₂ = A₂/A₁ = 0.5; temperature and emissivity do not determine view factors.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: Linearized radiation coefficient
questions.solution: The radiation coefficient is hr = εσ(Tₛ + Tsur)(Tₛ² + Tsur²). With Tₛ ≈ 473 K, Tsur ≈ 303 K, ε = 0.8 and σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸, hr ≈ 11.11 W/(m²·K). Do not use the overall 17.95 as the radiation coefficient.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: Definition of a gray body
questions.solution: A gray-body model has spectral emissivity independent of wavelength. A black body is the special ideal case with emissivity equal to one.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: Emissivity ratio in the printed identity
questions.solution: Among the printed options, ε = E/Eb is the emissivity definition and is the intended answer. The physical Kirchhoff law concerns equality of emissivity and absorptivity under the appropriate equilibrium/spectral conditions; the wording here is imprecise.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.editorial: The printed terminology is imprecise. Choose the intended emissivity ratio from the available options; the solution explains Kirchhoff’s law.

questions.title: Emittance of real bodies
questions.solution: For ordinary non-ideal radiating surfaces, total and spectral emissivities lie between zero and one. Unity describes an ideal black body. The printed symbol ε denotes emissivity here.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: View factors inside a square pyramid
questions.solution: The planar base has F₁₁ = 0. Symmetry makes its four side-face view factors equal. Their sum must be one, so each is 1/4 = 0.25.

sources.title: NPTEL · Radiation properties and view factors

questions.title: Counterflow effectiveness: 2017
questions.solution: For an adiabatic exchanger, Cₕ(250 − 100) = C꜀(80 − 50), so C꜀ = 5Cₕ and Cmin = Cₕ. Standard effectiveness ε = Q/[Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in)] = 150/(250 − 50) = 0.75. None of the four printed choices is correct; use the added corrected choice E.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat exchangers

questions.editorial: Printed option defect: none of A–D matches standard heat-exchanger effectiveness. Choice E is an editorial correction; the original screenshot is preserved.

questions.title: Counterflow effectiveness: 2018
questions.solution: Energy balance gives Cₕ × 120 = C꜀ × 55, so Cmin = Cₕ. Standard effectiveness ε = 120/(200 − 35) = 0.72727. The printed 0.33 is the cold-side temperature ratio, not standard exchanger effectiveness. The corrected choice E is added for graded practice.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat exchangers

questions.editorial: Printed option defect: none of A–D matches standard heat-exchanger effectiveness. Choice E is an editorial correction; the original screenshot is preserved.

questions.title: Heat-exchanger energy balance
questions.solution: The heat gained by water equals heat lost by gas: Q = 50 × 4.186 × (110 − 50) = 12558 kJ/min = 12.558 MJ/min. This is the magnitude of the gas enthalpy-rate decrease, nearest option C.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat exchangers

questions.title: Comparing fouling factors
questions.solution: Typical design tables give fuel-oil fouling resistance around 0.0009 m²·K/W, greater than the values for the other listed fluids under usual tabulated conditions. Fouling factors are empirical design values and vary with service conditions.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat exchangers

questions.title: Total heat transfer in a double-pipe exchanger
questions.solution: Compute directly from the water side: Q = (68/60) × 4180 × (75 − 35) = 189493.33 W = 189.49 kW. Oil heat capacity and overall U are unnecessary for this heat-duty calculation.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat exchangers

questions.title: Temperature and velocity effects on fouling
questions.solution: In the intended scaling/deposition trend, higher temperature promotes deposition and lower velocity reduces the surface shear that removes deposits. Thus increasing temperature and decreasing velocity tend to increase fouling. Actual trends depend on the fouling mechanism.

sources.title: NPTEL · Heat exchangers

questions.title: Solar-coating selectivity ratio
questions.solution: Solar selectivity is high solar-band absorptivity divided by low thermal-infrared emissivity: αsolar/εIR. This improves solar energy absorption while limiting thermal radiation loss.

sources.title: Tervo & Steiner · Spectrally selective solar absorbers

questions.title: Spectrally selective surface
questions.solution: A surface that strongly absorbs short-wave solar radiation while weakly emitting long-wave thermal radiation is spectrally selective. It is not a black body, which emits and absorbs strongly across all wavelengths.

sources.title: Tervo & Steiner · Spectrally selective solar absorbers
